titulo.en: Sound of the day: stress and the tilde

texto.en: Every Spanish word has one syllable that sounds stronger. If a word ends in a vowel, -n or -s, the stress falls on the next-to-last syllable: lunes, martes, jueves, viernes, domingo. When a word breaks that pattern, the stressed syllable carries a written accent mark called tilde (´): miércoles, sábado, música. So the tilde tells you where to push the voice: mi-ÉR-co-les, SÁ-ba-do, MÚ-si-ca. Say them slowly, stressing the syllable with the tilde.

To ask the time, say ¿Qué hora es? One o'clock is singular: Es la una. All other hours are plural: Son las dos, son las tres… son las doce. For minutes, add y cuarto (quarter past), y media (half past) or menos cuarto (quarter to): Son las tres y media = 3:30; Son las ocho menos cuarto = 7:45, so 8:45 is Son las nueve menos cuarto. To say at what time something happens, use a: ¿A qué hora es la clase? A las nueve. With one o'clock, a la una. Note that Spanish says Es la una y cuarto but Son las dos y cuarto. Days of the week do not use capital letters. Ask ¿Qué día es hoy? and answer Hoy es martes. To say on a day, use el: la clase es el martes; mañana es miércoles. From this class on, Emma and her teacher Sofía use tú with each other, because Sofía asks her to.
Tap each phrase to hear it. Only one o'clock is singular.
Tap each day to hear it. Days are written with a lowercase letter.

objetivo.en: Describe your morning and evening routine with reflexive verbs and say how often you do each thing.

nota.en: Ch sounds like the ch in “chair”.
The o changes to ue: me acuesto.

erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Yo me levanto a las seis.

explicacion.en: Levantarse is reflexive: you need the pronoun me before the verb. In English “I get up” has no extra word, but in Spanish it is me levanto.

erroresFrecuentes.incorrecto: Ella me ducha por la mañana.
erroresFrecuentes.correcto: Ella se ducha por la mañana.

explicacion.en: The reflexive pronoun must match the subject: yo me, tú te, ella se.
Acostarse changes o to ue in every form except nosotros: me acuesto, te acuestas, se acuesta. You will study this change in class 29.

texto.en: The Spanish ch sounds like the ch in the English word “chair”. It is one single sound, never a k or an sh. Practice it in the words of today: ducha, ducharse, noche, mucho. Say them slowly: DU-cha, du-CHAR-se, NO-che, MU-cho.

Many routine verbs are reflexive: levantarse (to get up), ducharse (to take a shower) and acostarse (to go to bed). They add a small pronoun that matches the subject: me (yo), te (tú), se (él, ella, usted, ellos, ellas, ustedes), nos (nosotros). The pronoun goes before the conjugated verb: Me levanto a las seis. ¿A qué hora te acuestas? In English you often drop it (“I get up”), but in Spanish it is required. Acostarse also changes o to ue: me acuesto, te acuestas, se acuesta, se acuestan, but nos acostamos. You will study this change in class 29. To say how often you do something, put siempre (always), a veces (sometimes) or nunca (never) before the verb: Siempre me levanto temprano. Nunca me acuesto tarde. Nunca already makes the sentence negative, so do not add no when it comes before the verb. To say “every day”, use todos los días; to say “on Saturdays”, use los sábados: Los sábados me levanto tarde.
Tap each form to hear it. The pronoun always goes before the verb.

objetivo.en: Say what time something starts and what you want, prefer or plan to do, and ask someone else the same.

nota.en: Pienso estudiar = I plan to study.

explicacion.en: In the yo form, the stem vowel e changes to ie: empiezo, not empezo.
The nosotros form does not change: queremos, preferimos, empezamos. The change happens only in the other forms.
After querer, preferir and pensar, put the infinitive directly. Do not add a or para: quiero comer, prefiero comer, pienso comer.

texto.en: In empiezo, quiero and prefiero, the two vowels i and e are said together as one single syllable, a diphthong. The ie sounds like the “ye” in “yes”: em-PYEH-so, KYEH-ro, pre-FYEH-ro. Do not split it into two syllables like “ee-eh”. Say them slowly: empiezo, quiero, prefiero, piensa.

Some verbs change the stem vowel e to ie when it is stressed: empezar (to start), querer (to want), preferir (to prefer) and pensar (to think, to plan). The change happens in yo, tú, él/ella/usted and ellos/ellas/ustedes: empiezo, empiezas, empieza, empiezan. In nosotros the stress falls on the ending, so there is no change: empezamos, queremos, preferimos, pensamos. Endings are the regular ones you know: -o, -as, -a, -amos, -an for empezar and pensar; -o, -es, -e, -emos, -en for querer; -o, -es, -e, -imos, -en for preferir. After querer, preferir and pensar, use an infinitive: Quiero desayunar. Prefiero comer temprano. Pienso estudiar hoy. Use pensar + infinitive to say what you plan to do. To ask a friend, say ¿Qué prefieres, café o té? and answer Prefiero café.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: c, z and s

texto.en: In Latin America the letters s, z, and c before e or i all sound the same, like the s in the English word “sit”: siesta, almuerzo, cena, cinco, doce. This is called seseo. In most of Spain, z and ce/ci sound like the th in “think”, but you do not need that sound here: use an s. Say the words of today slowly: al-MWER-so, SEH-na, SYEHS-ta, SEEN-ko, DOH-seh.

Some verbs change the stem vowel o to ue when it is stressed: almorzar (to have lunch), dormir (to sleep), volver (to come back) and poder (can, to be able to). As with e → ie, the change happens in yo, tú, él/ella/usted and ellos/ellas/ustedes: almuerzo, duermes, vuelve, pueden. Nosotros does not change: almorzamos, dormimos, volvemos, podemos. Use volver a + place to say where you come back to: Vuelvo a casa a las seis. After poder, use an infinitive: Puedo ayudar el domingo. Two useful questions: ¿A qué hora almuerzas? and ¿Cuántas horas duermes? Answer with a number: Duermo siete horas. Remember: acostarse, which you saw in class 27, also changes o to ue: me acuesto.

objetivo.en: Say what you like or love to do in your free time (singular and plural) and agree with another person.

explicacion.en: Gustar agrees with the thing you like: one thing, me gusta; several things, me gustan. Deportes is plural, so use gustan.
In English the person is the subject (“I like”), but in Spanish the thing liked is the subject: me gusta bailar literally means “dancing pleases me”.
An infinitive counts as a single idea: use gusta, even with two verbs. Use gustan only for plural nouns.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: gu and qu

texto.en: In the groups gue, gui, que and qui, the letter u is silent. It only helps the g keep its hard sound (as in “go”): guitarra sounds like “ghee-TAH-rra”. In the same way, qu always sounds like a plain k, so ¿quién? sounds like “kyen”. But in gusta the g is followed by u and then s, so the u is pronounced: “GOOS-ta”. Say them slowly: me gusta, la guitarra, ¿quién?

titulo.en: I like it, I love it: gustar and encantar

texto.en: In Spanish, the thing you like is the subject of the verb. So gustar and encantar agree with it. For one thing or for an action, use gusta and encanta: Me gusta el fútbol. Me encanta bailar. For several things, use gustan and encantan: Me gustan los deportes. Me encantan los partidos. Encantar is stronger: it means “to love”. Change the pronoun for the person: me (I), te (you, tú), le (he, she, usted): ¿Te gustan los deportes? A don Jorge le gusta el fútbol. To agree with someone, use A mí también after something affirmative (Me gusta bailar. A mí también.) and A mí tampoco after something negative (No me gusta correr. A mí tampoco.).
